Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC

1. Parse the grid, caps, and action schema. Treat each instance as independent and use only its demonstrations. Follow the game protocol literally: make no ancillary tool calls, and reply with only one allowed action JSON—no narration, formatting, or other text. Treat each demo as evidence, not a superficial template.
2. Compare every demo input/output cell-by-cell, including unchanged cells. Infer output dimensions and the exact spatial mapping for roles, boundaries, direction, extent, and collisions; verify every region, row, and column against each pair before applying it. For periodic/diagonal patterns, derive an explicit coordinate rule (modulus, orientation, phase) and verify successive rows and columns. For copied, tiled, or transformed regions, verify the proposed operation explicitly (including rotation direction) rather than assuming a repeated, mirrored, or globally uniform pattern; do not extend a rule to test-only values or layouts unsupported by demos. Never infer a stripe, translation, reflection, fill, or expansion rule from resemblance alone.
3. For line-completion puzzles, verify the exact completion geometry from demos: determine whether gaps are filled only between collinear endpoints, whether endpoints can be in separate segments, and whether existing markers interrupt or bound lines. Check horizontal and vertical behavior separately, and preserve all cells not changed by the demonstrated rule. Do not extrapolate every row/column between global extrema unless the demo establishes that.
4. Request a demo only if you can name at least two plausible rules and the predicted outputs that distinguish them; weigh this information against demo cost. After receiving it, explicitly eliminate or retain the alternatives. Avoid additional demos when the examples already establish a consistent rule or no specific distinction remains.
5. After an incorrect submission, reassess the whole mapping against all demos and identify the unsupported assumption. Do not repeat or tweak a failed candidate without evidence distinguishing the new rule. If still underdetermined, request a targeted demo only when you can state plausible alternatives and what input/output feature would distinguish them; weigh its cost against the chance of resolving the ambiguity. Do not burn submissions on near-identical guesses or spend a demo when it cannot discriminate the rules.
6. Before each action, check remaining caps and cost. Before submitting, explicitly count the output rows and the cells in every row; confirm they match the inferred height and width, and that every cell is an integer from 0 to 9. Do not rely on visual alignment or copy a row with an unchecked cell count. Then output only the one allowed action JSON. Request demos with the exact action; use finish only after the instance is over.

# Continual-ARC

1. Parse the grid, caps, and action schema. Treat each instance as independent and use only its demonstrations. Follow the game protocol literally: make no ancillary tool calls, and reply with only one allowed action JSON—no narration, formatting, or other text. Treat each demo as evidence, not a superficial template.
2. Compare every demo input/output cell-by-cell, including unchanged cells. Infer output dimensions and the exact spatial mapping for roles, boundaries, direction, extent, and collisions; verify every region, row, and column against each pair before applying it. For periodic/diagonal patterns, derive an explicit coordinate rule (modulus, orientation, phase) and verify successive rows and columns. For copied, tiled, or transformed regions, verify the proposed operation explicitly (including rotation direction) rather than assuming a repeated, mirrored, or globally uniform pattern; do not extend a rule to test-only values or layouts unsupported by demos. Never infer a stripe, translation, reflection, fill, or expansion rule from resemblance alone.
3. For line-completion puzzles, verify the exact completion geometry from demos: determine whether gaps are filled only between collinear endpoints, whether endpoints can be in separate segments, and whether existing markers interrupt or bound lines. Check horizontal and vertical behavior separately, and preserve all cells not changed by the demonstrated rule. Do not extrapolate every row/column between global extrema unless the demo establishes that.
4. Request a demo only if you can name at least two plausible rules and the predicted outputs that distinguish them; weigh this information against demo cost. After receiving it, explicitly eliminate or retain the alternatives. Avoid additional demos when the examples already establish a consistent rule or no specific distinction remains.
5. After an incorrect submission, reassess the whole mapping against all demos and identify the unsupported assumption. Do not repeat or tweak a failed candidate without evidence distinguishing the new rule. If still underdetermined, request a targeted demo only when you can state plausible alternatives and what input/output feature would distinguish them; weigh its cost against the chance of resolving the ambiguity. Do not burn submissions on near-identical guesses or spend a demo when it cannot discriminate the rules.
6. Before each action, check remaining caps and cost. Before submitting, explicitly count the output rows and the cells in every row; confirm they match the inferred height and width, and that every cell is an integer from 0 to 9. Do not rely on visual alignment or copy a row with an unchecked cell count. Then output only the one allowed action JSON. Request demos with the exact action; use finish only after the instance is over.
